         COMES NOW, Cherokee Creek Partners, Bonnie Helene McAnelly, Individually and as

Trustee of the 2025 Homestead Trust and The Bonnie Helene McAnelly 2023 Trust, Bernareggio

Family Partners, Ltd., Robert Bowling, and Wendell and Shirley Fleming (“Cherokee Creek

Aligned Intervenors”) and files their Post-Hearing Initial Brief (the “Post-Hearing Initial Brief”)

to the Application of Oncor and LCRA TSC (“Joint Applicants,” or “Oncor” and “LCRA TSC,”

respectively) for the above to amend their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity (“CCN” or

“Application”). Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors pray that the Administrative Law Judge

(“ALJ”) issue a Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) recommending the Texas Public Utility

Commission (“PUC”) approve Cherokee Creek Route G (“Route CCG”).

                                      I.         INTRODUCTION

        The Bell County East Switch to Big Hill project is a proposed single-circuit transmission

line between the 765/345-kV expansion at Oncor’s existing Bell County East Switch, located 5.5

miles southeast of the City of Temple in Bell County, Texas, and the 765/345-kV expansion of

LCRA TSC’s existing Big Hill 345-kV Substation, located 13 miles northeast of the City of

Eldorado in Schleicher County, Texas. Jointly developed by LCRA and Oncor, the project would

be one of the most powerful transmission lines ever built in the state, operating at the highest

voltage the State has ever seen. The route traverses some of Texas’ most treasured and ecologically

sensitive landscapes, passing through portions of the Edwards Plateau, the Hill Country, and the

wide-open ranchlands of West Texas. That makes responsible routing not just a legal obligation,

but a matter of public responsibility and stewardship.

        Under PURA § 37.056(c), in granting a certificate of convenience and necessity, the

Commission shall consider “community values, recreational and park areas, historical and


Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors Initial Post-Hearing Brief

Page 3
 aesthetic values, [and] environmental integrity.” In addition to considering these factors, the

Commission includes engineering constraints, costs, prudent avoidance, paralleling, and routing

the line to moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners, in its routing analysis.1

        Throughout this brief, the Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors rely on the quartile analysis

developed by their environmental expert, Rae Lynn Schneider Reinecke (“Reinecke”). Her

analysis provides a consistent and structured framework for comparing route performance across

the numerous environmental and land use criteria evaluated in the Environmental Assessment’s

Table 7-2. 2 Because the Environmental Assessment (“EA”) itself contains no ranking system or

comparative methodology, the quartile framework fills a critical tool in the record by giving the

Commission a proportionate way to evaluate what the raw data actually shows.

        Reinecke’s quartile analysis divides all 123 alternative routes (the 122 routes filed with the

Application plus Route CCG) groups for each routing criterion evaluated in EA Table 7-2. 3 Routes

in Quartile 1 fall within the lowest 25th percentile of values on a given criterion, while routes in

Quartile 4 fall within the highest 25th percentile. 4 Whether a lower or higher quartile is favorable

depends on the resource category: for some criteria, a lower value is desirable (e.g., fewer habitable

structures), while for others a higher value is preferable (e.g., greater distance from residences). 5

This approach enables the Commission to assess whether a route performs comparatively well,

moderately, or poorly across the entire universe of alternatives, rather than evaluating raw numbers

        This matters because PURA § 37.056(c) and PUC Rule § 25.101(b)(3)(B) require the

Commission to evaluate multiple statutory routing factors together, including community values,

recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, landowner

impacts, and compatible land use. No single criterion controls, and the Commission must weigh

the relative performance of each route across all of them. Reinecke’s quartile analysis provides the

framework the Commission needs to conduct the holistic evaluation the PUC Substantive Rule

requires. Routes that perform well across categories emerge as genuinely preferable alternatives,

while routes that accumulate adverse rankings across categories reveal the true scope of their

impacts.

           Under such framework, the record evidence compellingly supports Route CCG. The

analysis detailed in Reineke’s testimony demonstrates that Route CCG avoids United States Fish

& Wildlife Service (“USFWS”) Karst Zone 1 (areas known to contain endangered karst

invertebrate species) entirely and avoids the Edwards Aquifer, addressing two of the most

significant regulatory and ecological constraints in the eastern Study Area. 8 Route CCG encounters

substantially fewer parks and recreational resources within proximity bands that matter most to

visual and recreational impact: within 0.5 to 1 mile, Route CCG has no parkland acreage, while

Route 894 has 442.65 acres; within 1 to 2 miles, Route CCG has 105.27 parkland acres compared

Golden-cheeked Warbler (“GCW”) habitat than Route 894, an advantage that takes on added

weight given Texas Parks and Wildlife Department’s (“TPWD”) explicit recommendation to avoid

routing through suitable GCW habitat. 10 Route CCG would result in approximately 438 fewer

acres of vegetation clearing within fragmentation-sensitive habitats. 11 At the major river crossings,

Route CCG optimizes alignment by utilizing an existing pipeline corridor at the Colorado River

and an existing transmission line at the San Saba River. 12

           Route CCG is not a perfect route. No route of this scale can avoid all impacts. But

perfection is not the standard PURA or the PUC Substantive Rule requires. The standard is a

reasonable balance of the applicable routing criteria. Criterion by criterion, that balance favors

Route CCG. The Commission should approve it.

           PUC Procedural Rule 22.52 governs notice requirements for electric licensing proceedings.

This includes (a)(1) newspaper notices, (a)(2) municipalities, counties, Department of Defense

Military Aviation and Installation Assurance Siting Clearinghouse, (a)(3) directly impacted

landowners, (4)(a) notices for at least one public meeting to be had prior to the filing of the

Application. Specifically, this notice provision, no matter to whom or what it applies, requires the

Applicant to include the following language: “All routes and route segments included in this

notice are available for selection and approval by the Public Utility Commission of Texas.” At

the Hearing on the Merits, Ms. Brenda Perkins confirmed that language was included in the notices

by the Joint Applicants, that the Joint Applicants would construct Route CCG if ordered, and that

in her 30 years of experience in transmission line routing cases, the Commission has ordered routes

comprising of noticed segments, even if those routes were not included in the Application. 13

Furthermore, PUC Staff witness, John Poole, included Route CCG in its analysis, considers it a

viable route for selection by the PUC, confirmed that the Commission in the past has selected RFI

routes, and that he had no notice concerns about any Cherokee Creek RFI route. 14

           Colorado River Alliance’s reliance on Rule 22.52 to challenge RFI routes that were

developed during the discovery and hearing process improperly conflates the initial notice

requirements with the ongoing, iterative development through which routing alternatives are

developed and refined in contested-case proceedings.

 C. PUBLIC INPUT
 1. What were the principal concerns expressed in the questionnaire responses received
    at or after any public meetings held by the applicant regarding the proposed
    transmission facilities?

         The Joint Applicants conducted public outreach, including 3 public open house meetings

attended by a total of 825 individuals and received 189 questionnaire responses at the meetings

themselves, with numerous additional questionnaires, letters, and electronic mail communications

received afterward from individuals, groups, landowners, and officials. 15 The community input

gathered through the Joint Applicants’ public outreach process reflects a striking and consistent

message: the communities in the Bell County East Switch to Big Hill study area place the

protection of natural resources, the Hill Country’s aesthetic character, agricultural land, and private

property above all else. Respondents across all three meetings raised mutually reinforcing

concerns, including proximity of proposed routes to residences; impacts to ranching and farming

operations; aesthetic harm to Hill Country viewsheds; effects on property values; health concerns

regarding electromagnetic fields; threats to fish, wildlife, and endangered species; and the

importance of historic resources. 16 As the EA summarized, many respondents were concerned

about natural resources specifically, including impacts on the San Gabriel River, the Lampasas

River, and the San Saba River and other streams in the Study Area, threatened and endangered

species such as the Golden-cheeked Warbler and black-capped vireo, wildlife migration routes,

erosion, and the Edwards Aquifer recharge zone. 17

E. ROUTE

    which proposed transmission-line route is the best alternative?

             a. Statutory criteria

                    i.    Community Values; PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)

        The Commission has interpreted “community values” as “a shared appreciation of an area

or other natural or human resource by a national, regional, or local community.” 18 The community

values expressed in this record are not abstract preferences, but documented, quantified, and

specific concerns.

        In addition to summary findings of questionnaires received by the Joint Applicants in the

EA, as discussed in the above Public Input section, Reinecke conducted a systematic review of

public engagement materials, logging and evaluating 3,793 individual filings submitted to the PUC

Interchange for Docket No. 59475. 19 Her review encompassed all items filed with a timestamp at

or prior to 5:00 p.m. Central Standard Time on May 11, 2026, with Item No. 3793 as the list item.

Of those filings, she classified 1,580 as unique intervenors, 950 as protest forms, and 654 as

opposition letters, excluding 101 duplicate filings from her analysis. 20 Her findings were that

“most commentors were generally in opposition to the overall project and alignment through the

        At the public open house meetings, questionnaire respondents ranked routing criteria using

a weighted scoring system in three categories: land use, paralleling, and distance from community

resources. 22 For land use priorities (Question 5), the highest-ranked criterion was minimizing the

length across residential areas (weighted score: 2,689), followed closely by minimizing the

visibility of the line (2,648) and minimizing the length across pastureland (2,431). 23 For distance

from community resources (Question 7), respondents most strongly prioritized maximizing

distance from residences (3,913), followed by maximizing distance from schools (2,250),

historical and archaeological sites (2,137), and parks and recreational areas (2,117). 24 Notably,

paralleling-related metrics were addressed in a separate question (Question 6), with maximizing

distance along existing transmission line corridors ranking first among that category (1,893),

followed by existing roadway corridors (1,592) and railroad corridors (1,488). 25 Among

organizational participants, the Friends of the San Saba River submitted concerns related to

flooding, wildlife, and river crossings; the Edwards Plateau Alliance and the Hill Country Land &

Legacy Alliance also filed items in the docket expressing opposition to the project. 26

        Reinecke conducted an independent analysis of Questions 5, 6, and 7 and found that key

indicators favored Route CCG over Route 894, including: (1) minimizing distance through

residential areas, (2) minimizing visibility, (3) maximizing compatible right-of-way (“ROW”)

        Reinecke’s analysis of the full public record demonstrates that community concerns

encompassed far more than proximity to residences. Taken together, the record demonstrates that

communities throughout the Study Area consistently expressed concerns rooted in environmental

integrity, including protection of rivers and riparian systems, wildlife and endangered species

habitat, and sensitive natural landscapes, that extend well beyond the narrower metric of proximity

to parks and recreational land. Reinecke’s analysis is the most comprehensive and

methodologically rigorous assessment of community values in evidence, grounding her routing

conclusions in the full documented weight of public opinion rather than generalized impressions.

        Route CCG addresses those concerns directly: it avoids the Edwards Aquifer, avoids

USFWS Karst Zone 1, avoids the ESSS portion of the Colorado River and the Rocky Creek ESSS

crossed by Route 894, crosses the San Saba River at a preferable existing-infrastructure location,

avoids USFWS-designated critical habitat for the Texas fatmucket (Lampsilis bracteata)

associated with Cherokee Creek, and would result in approximately 438 fewer acres of vegetation

clearing within fragmentation-sensitive habitats compared to Route 894. 28 Route CCG also

addresses the organizational concerns of the NRCS and TPWD regarding GCW conservation

priorities, the TPWD Texas State Parks viewshed concerns, and the Friends of the San Saba

River’s preliminary link objections. 29

        Under GIS-based distance-band analysis, the spatial distribution of park and recreational

                                           IV.      CONCLUSION
        Reinecke's testimony and analysis stands alone in this proceeding. No other expert undertook

a systematic, quantitative and qualitative review of the alternative routes using a consistent

comparative framework. Her quartile analysis exposes what raw data cannot: Route CCG

outperforms the alternatives. On paralleling, Route CCG consolidates disturbance within existing

corridors at both major river crossings, following an existing pipeline at the Colorado River and an

existing transmission line at the San Saba -- a choice Route 894 and Route 487 ignores. On

community values, Reinecke's review of 3,793 individual PUC filings -- the only comprehensive

review in the record -- documents a quantified public preference for minimizing visibility,

maximizing distance from residences, and protecting natural resources that Route CCG satisfies and

Route 894 and 487 does not. Route CCG best protects Colorado State Bend Park and Post Oak Ridge

State Park by routing the transmission lines farther away making less of a visual impact. Route

CCG's slightly higher cost is only 4.4% higher than Route 894, and its habitable structure count

remains at the lower end of the dataset, rendering neither factors a meaningful basis for rejection.

On environmental integrity, Route CCG avoids the Edwards Aquifer, avoids the ESSS-designated

reach of the Colorado River and Rocky Creek, crosses fewer miles of Golden-cheeked Warbler

habitat, and clears 438 fewer acres of fragmentation-sensitive habitat. Criterion by criterion, the

record favors Route CCG. No other route in this proceeding matches Route CCG's balance of

performance across this full range of criteria.
